summary: A paper examining the next-generation IP effort from the perspective of very large corporations that have invested heavily in TCP/IP to meet business goals. It looks at what such users would need from a new IP. It is informational input to the IPng discussion.

eli5.summary: Big companies explain what they need from the new internet rules so their business keeps running while things change.

questions: what do large companies want from ipng
what does a large company need from ipng
corporate requirements for next generation ip
subtitle: What large corporations need from the next-generation internet protocol

tldr.problem: Large corporations had invested heavily in IPv4 and TCP/IP for internal networks and questioned whether they needed a replacement protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents five key corporate requirements for IPng: piecemeal transition support, support for technological advances, convergence with international standards, plug-and-play networking, and better security than IPv4.
tldr.outcome: The document highlights that corporations primarily buy applications, not networking technologies, so IPng deployment depends on whether killer applications require it or if senior management mandates it.

today: RFC 1687 is Informational and presents a corporate user perspective from 1994. The subsequent adoption of IPv6 has been slower than expected, and many large corporations continue to use IPv4 alongside limited IPv6 deployment, validating the RFC's analysis that corporations prioritize business needs over protocol upgrades.

sections.title: Corporate Perspective on IPng
sections.content:
This RFC presents the viewpoint of large corporations on the proposed next-generation IP protocol. Unlike the IETF community, which saw IPng as an essential upgrade to address IPv4's address space limitations, large end users viewed IPng with skepticism. The author, from Boeing Computer Services, explains that corporate users generally do not see the Internet's scalability problems as sufficient motivation to deploy an entirely new protocol within their own private networks.

The central question is simple: what benefits justify the expense of deploying IPng? The RFC identifies that corporate users are primarily driven by business needs, not technological improvements. Users buy applications, not networking technologies.
sections.eli5: Big companies like Boeing did not think they needed the new internet rules just because scientists said the old ones had problems. They would only switch if new computer programs absolutely needed it.

sections.title: Why Corporations See TCP/IP and the Internet Differently
sections.content:
The RFC highlights a fundamental difference in perspective between the IETF community and large corporate users. The IETF closely associates TCP/IP with the Internet and views them as nearly inseparable. However, corporations view them very differently. Many large companies have deployed TCP/IP extensively without depending on Internet connectivity. Some corporations have TCP/IP networks with only a tiny percentage of hosts that have direct Internet access.

Corporations have made substantial investments in their own external communication infrastructures and conduct core business processes through private networks, not the public Internet. This means that the Internet's address depletion problem and IPv4 scalability concerns do not directly impact most of a corporation's internal TCP/IP hosts.
sections.eli5: Companies have their own private networks that are separate from the public Internet. The problems with the public Internet do not affect their private networks, so they do not care as much about fixing the Internet's problems.

sections.title: Corporate Security Islands and Access Control
sections.content:
The IETF generally views firewalls and security islands as undesirable obstacles to global connectivity. Corporations have the opposite perspective. They treat data as a sensitive corporate asset and restrict access carefully. Different employee classes need different levels of access, and critical corporate systems must never be accessible from outside the company.

Corporations partition hosts into three categories: those without Internet access, those with limited Internet services through application relays, and those with unlimited Internet access. Security islands are one mechanism corporations use to enforce these boundaries and protect their most valuable systems. This security-first approach reflects corporate values of data protection and risk management, which differ fundamentally from the IETF's goal of universal, unrestricted connectivity.
sections.eli5: Companies keep their most important computers locked away and only let certain employees and programs access them. They view firewalls as protection, not as barriers to remove.

sections.title: Five Key Corporate Requirements for IPng
sections.content:
The RFC presents five requirements corporations would need IPng to meet before widespread adoption becomes likely. First, corporations need piecemeal transition support. Given that large deployments might include tens of thousands of TCP/IP hosts, complete migration is unrealistic. IPng and IPv4 must coexist indefinitely, with internal communication between both populations.

Second, IPng must not hinder technological advances. Third, IPng should foster synergy with International Standards (OSI), which some industries like aviation require for regulatory compliance. Fourth, corporations need plug-and-play or self-defining networks that auto-configure and auto-address without manual overhead. Fifth, IPng must offer better security than IPv4, with integrated, effective security mechanisms across all vendors' implementations.
sections.eli5: Companies want IPng to work alongside the old system, not replace it. They want networks that set themselves up automatically and keep data safer than before. Some industries also need it to match international standards.

sections.title: What Actually Motivates Corporate Deployment
sections.content:
Despite the corporate requirements listed, the RFC identifies only two realistic motivations for widespread corporate adoption of IPng. First, corporations will deploy IPng if killer applications emerge that provide critical new functionality IPv4 cannot deliver—such as real-time applications, multimedia capabilities, or scalable plug-and-play networking. Such applications must provide significant business benefits to justify the deployment and support costs.

Second, corporations might adopt IPng if it achieves convergence with International Standards (OSI). This would provide a single standard for both Internet and international commerce, potentially reducing the protocol diversity and complexity that large corporations must support. Without one of these two major drivers, corporations will continue using IPv4 indefinitely, even after IPng becomes widely available on the Internet.
sections.eli5: Companies will only switch to the new system if they get amazing new programs that need it, or if one standard covers both the Internet and international trade.

references.text: Bradner, S., Ed., "IP: Next Generation (IPng) White Paper Solicitation", RFC 1550, December 1993.
